--- TEXT ---
Causation cannot be adequately analyzed as mere regular succession between types of events because regularity is too indiscriminate. If one event type is regularly followed by another, that fact alone does not show that the first produces, generates, or makes a difference to the second. A falling barometer reading is regularly followed by a storm, but the falling reading does not cause the storm. Rather, both are effects of a common atmospheric condition: changes in air pressure. The regular sequence is real, but it is not causal in the relevant direction. This shows that a regularity account mistakes reliable association for causal connection. It lacks the resources to distinguish cases in which one event genuinely brings about another from cases in which the two are merely correlated because of a shared background cause or accidental pattern.

Interventionist accounts, especially as developed by James Woodward, succeed at precisely this point by analyzing causation in terms of stable dependence under ideal interventions. On this view, the crucial question is not whether events of one type are regularly followed by events of another type, but whether changing the putative cause by an appropriate intervention would change the effect. A causal relation exists when the effect depends on the cause in a way that remains invariant under interventions that alter the cause while holding fixed other relevant influences. If one could intervene to change the barometer reading alone, without changing the atmospheric conditions, the storm would not thereby be changed. By contrast, if one intervenes on a genuine cause, the effect varies accordingly. The interventionist account therefore captures the difference-making structure that regular succession by itself misses.

This also explains the epistemic privilege of randomized controlled experiments. Such experiments are powerful because their design approximates an ideal intervention on the putative cause. Random assignment severs the treatment or exposure from its ordinary antecedents, preventing preexisting differences among subjects from determining who receives the intervention. As a result, correlations between the assigned treatment and the outcome are not merely ordinary regularities embedded in a web of background causes; they are evidence of what happens when the putative cause is manipulated independently. The randomized controlled experiment is therefore especially well suited to reveal causal relations because it creates conditions under which the relevant dependency can be observed apart from the confounding patterns that make regular succession insufficient.
--- END ---
